The numbers behind the collapse.

The rial-to-dollar exchange rate has gone from 32,000 to 1 in 2018 to roughly 1.4 million to 1 in 2026. That's a 97% loss in purchasing power in 8 years.

The Iranian government maintains an official rate that's roughly 90% stronger than the parallel market rate. The official rate is fictional. Almost no actual transactions happen at it.

The parallel market rate is what determines what Iranians can actually buy.

Sanctions cut off Iran's access to international banking. Oil revenue dropped 70%+ from peak. Foreign reserves depleted. The government printed currency to fund domestic spending. Inflation accelerated past 50% annual rate.

Each factor compounds the others.

What this means for ordinary Iranians.

Both paths are visible in the regime's recent behavior.

The Trump administration's blockade is accelerating the timeline. Each week of continued blockade pushes the rial weaker. Each weakening of the rial increases population stress. Each stress increase pushes the regime toward decision.

The population that wanted regime change for 47 years is now closer to seeing it than at any point since 1979.

The rial collapse is the leading indicator.

72 cents to a million rials. The math tells the story.

While the country had diversified beyond oil, structural weaknesses left it vulnerable to the shocks of the current war. 

Macroeconomic Indicators (Pre-2026 War)
Galloping Inflation: Official annual inflation remained above 40% throughout 2025.

Currency Collapse: The rial faced constant depreciation, necessitating the introduction of a 10-million rial banknote just before the war to keep up with price hikes.

Digital Economy: A growing digital sector accounted for 5 - 6% of GDP before internet shutdowns during the conflict crippled these businesses.

Economic hardship and rial devaluations triggered massive anti-government protests and strikes in early 2026, leading to a violent state crackdown.

text:
The Regime Will Destroy Iran to Save Itself
Iran’s Foreign Minister announced on April 17 that the Strait of Hormuz is open to commercial vessels for the duration of the ceasefire. Brent crude fell 10 percent. WTI dropped 12 percent. Trump said Iran has “agreed to everything,” including removing its enriched uranium. Iran disputes this. Iranian officials say transferring uranium to the U.S. “has not been an option.” The regime made concessions under financial pressure. It has not surrendered.

The regime is not acting as a single actor. The Foreign Minister is de-escalating to survive the cash crisis. IRGC hardliners are publicly contradicting him. They see any concession as treason. The conflicting statements are not diplomacy. They are a regime coming apart at the seams.

Any agreement Iran reaches with Trump should be viewed through the lens of Taqiyya — the Shia doctrine that permits deception of non-Muslims when the regime’s survival is at stake. The regime is not negotiating in good faith. It is buying time it no longer has.

The regime’s coercive apparatus runs on cash. The cash has stopped moving. The first break appeared in the regime’s ability to turn barrels into usable money.

The regime cannot reverse this sequence without sanctions relief, access to foreign reserves, and an end to the blockade. Trump will grant none of them short of full surrender.

Trump posted on Truth Social: “It’s not politically correct to use the term, ‘Regime Change,’ but if the current Iranian Regime is unable to MAKE IRAN GREAT AGAIN, why wouldn’t there be a Regime change???”

Operation “Economic” Epic Fury
The regime is being strangled by the loss of its own oil revenue.

Oil Export Revenue
Oil and gas normally provide 60% of Iranian government revenue and 80% of export earnings. Iran exported 1.84 million barrels per day in March 2026 and 1.71 million bpd in early April. Those numbers are deceptive.
Iran’s true pre-war baseline was lower: 1.48 million bpd in 2024 and 1.69 million bpd in 2025. The wartime figures were inflated by barrels pushed into floating storage before the choke tightened. They did not show usable cash reaching the regime. They showed only a delay before financial collapse.

Trump’s naval blockade began at 10:00 a.m. Eastern on April 13 and immediately started choking off exports. More than 180 million barrels of Iranian oil sat in floating storage. The barrels had moved. The cash had not. The state lost its main funding source at the same moment the IRGC — which controls roughly 50% of Iran’s oil exports — lost its primary revenue stream.

Disruption of Hormuz Traffic
Since February 28, Iran has shut the Strait of Hormuz to all vessels except its own and attempted to impose tolls of $1 to $2 million per vessel, payable in Chinese yuan. Pre-war commercial traffic of 100 to 120 vessels per day collapsed to a trickle. The International Maritime Organization called the tolls unlawful. Maersk, CMA CGM, and Hapag-Lloyd suspended transits. The artery that once moved Iran’s oil to market became the artery the regime weaponized against itself.

Currency Collapse
The rial now trades between 1.5 and 1.66 million per dollar on the free market. Bonbast showed 1,589,500 rials per dollar on April 12. The Central Bank issued a 10 million rial note in March — the largest denomination in Iranian history — one month after issuing the 5 million note. The rial has lost 99% of its value since 1979. The acceleration in 2026 is the final stage.
Inflation

Official annual inflation reached 50.6% for the 12 months ending March 20, 2026. Food inflation hit 105% by February. Bread rose 18% in the first quarter. Rice rose 12%. Some staples increased sevenfold. At this level, inflation destroys the value of every salary the regime still pays.

Bank Stress and Cash Shortage
Bank Sepah — the bank that processes IRGC and military payroll — had its main data center struck on March 11. Iranian banks now impose informal daily withdrawal caps of 30 to 50 million rials — roughly $18 to $30 per customer. Cash in circulation rose 23% in eight months and surged 49% year-over-year by January 2026 due to panic hoarding. The system that delivers pay has been physically destroyed. The system that holds savings is rationing them.

Running Out of Storage
Iran normally exports around 1.5 million barrels per day through the Strait of Hormuz — roughly 40% of the government budget. One-third of that oil directly funds the IRGC and the armed forces. The oil must move. Tankers must empty to return for loading. Iran has only about two weeks of onshore storage. If tankers cannot leave and onshore storage fills, extraction shuts down. Shut-in causes permanent damage to reservoir pressure. The oil that stays in the ground today may never come out.

The Self-Inflicted Wound
The regime damaged itself more than the war did. By shutting or threatening the Strait of Hormuz and trying to impose tolls, it turned its main revenue source into a weapon against itself. Tankers refused the route. Insurance rates spiked. Buyers walked away. Settlements froze. China’s Iranian crude imports significantly in early 2026. The discount Iran had to offer to keep remaining buyers widened. The IRGC collected some tolls. The government lost net oil export revenue several times greater than the toll income.

This is the largest self-inflicted economic wound in the Islamic Republic’s history. The regime discovered that buyers do not pay coerced premiums. They find other suppliers and other routes.

The Payroll Crisis
The regime survives on a loyalty-for-cash model. The cash is failing.
Police special units have been paid late three times this year and refused to attend pro-government rallies. Army retirees and active Artesh personnel have gone unpaid for two consecutive months as of mid-March. The Basij, leaderless after the killing of Commander General Gholamreza Soleimani on March 17, has lost its per-task funding. Air force pilots are reluctant to fly combat missions. The IRGC is recalling retirees, offering prisoners amnesty in exchange for service, and recruiting twelve-year-olds. The Basij is using seventh-graders.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated on April 9 that defections are happening “at all levels.” Iran International reported 350 personnel left a single police base. In some units, absence or desertion rates approach 90 percent. The IRGC and the Artesh are in open conflict, with the IRGC refusing to evacuate wounded Artesh soldiers.
The internet blackout and regime propaganda have produced a security apparatus and population largely out of touch with reality on the ground. Iran’s mosaic command structure — 31 separate regional commands — is fragmented and insulated. Many mid- and lower-level commanders and Basij units remain unaware of how badly the United States and Israel have destroyed Iran’s ability to wage war or project power and terrorism to its neighbors and beyond. This information vacuum keeps them motivated. They will suppress protests, shoot civilians, and defend checkpoints even when the war is clearly lost.

The IRGC’s dual funding stream — state budget plus its commercial empire through Khatam al-Anbiya — historically insulated it from fiscal crises. That insulation is gone. The state budget is collapsing as oil revenue drops to zero. The commercial empire is constrained by sanctions, war damage, and the Bank Sepah strike. Both streams are failing at the same time.

What Cannot Survive Without Pay
Top IRGC command and the patronage elites can survive briefly. They have offshore assets, smuggling networks, real estate holdings, and bonyad revenue.

Everyone else cannot. Police, riot police, regular Artesh, conscript-level IRGC, and Basij rank-and-file depend on monthly cash. When the cash stops, the chain breaks. Mid-level commanders act independently. Local units negotiate their own arrangements. Some defect. Some go into business for themselves through smuggling and extortion. The state stops being one system and becomes a collection of armed franchises.

The pattern is consistent across every authoritarian collapse. The Soviet Union in 1991. Gaddafi in 2011. Mubarak in 2011. Yanukovych in 2014. Assad in 2024. Every regime that lost the ability to pay its coercive apparatus broke within 60 to 120 days. The breaking point was never the size of the protests. It was the defection of mid-level security officers.

30 / 60 / 90 Day Outlook
The traditional signs of regime collapse — mass street protests and bazaar shutdowns — already occurred in late 2025 and January 2026. The regime answered with massacre. The collapse mechanism from here is mid-level security officer defection driven by payroll failure. The next uprising will come, but only after the security forces lose the financial incentive to stop it.

30 Days
The blockade chokes off remaining oil exports and toll revenue. Bank Sepah’s cash crisis deepens. Lower-tier IRGC, Basij, and Artesh salaries arrive late or partial. The IRGC tries to compensate through money printing and bonyad revenue, but rial-denominated pay loses 3 to 5 percent of real purchasing power per month at current inflation. Tehran prices rise sharply. The internet blackout slows protest coordination but kills digital payments and commercial activity. It buys the regime time on the street while costing it time on the economy.
The Basij rank-and-file is doing the math. Checkpoint duty pays less every week. The regime’s capacity to suppress the next round of protests is degrading with every paycheck.

60 Days
If the blockade holds and ground operations against Kharg or Abu Musa proceed, IRGC revenue from Hormuz tolls reaches zero. Oil revenue approaches zero. Hard currency reserves of $20 to $30 billion drain at $3 to $5 billion per month, though actual accessible liquid reserves are likely far lower. Payroll for security forces fails systematically. The regime keeps sending rials. The rials no longer buy food, fuel, or medicine at prices security personnel can survive on. Patronage networks fracture. Mid-level commanders begin acting independently — some negotiating with opposition figures, some turning to smuggling and extortion. Elites accelerate capital flight.

90 Days
Sustained financial squeeze with no sanctions relief, no blockade end, and no Chinese rescue. Four possible outcomes emerge.

The most likely is a palace coup by an IRGC faction seeking a deal with the U.S. to preserve its position and wealth, sacrificing Mojtaba Khamenei and the clerical structure.
Second is collapse into multi-polar armed competition between IRGC factions, the Artesh, and opposition militias from Kurdish regions, Sistan-Baluchestan, and Arab Khuzestan.

Third is negotiated exit with mass defection of mid-level officers and rapid disintegration of the command structure.
Fourth and least likely is regime survival through Chinese emergency financial intervention and IRGC consolidation under a single faction that accepts Trump’s terms. This would require China to break from its current pattern of diplomatic-only support and commit hard currency at scale. Nothing in Chinese behavior to date supports this outcome.

The Mechanism of Collapse
The most likely path is an IRGC palace coup. A faction within senior IRGC command, seeking to preserve its institutional power and personal wealth, cuts a deal with the United States. It sacrifices Mojtaba Khamenei and the remaining clerical leadership and accepts terms it rejected in Islamabad. The bargain trades the regime for the wealth its leaders extracted over four decades.
The alternative is fragmentation. Provincial commanders break from Tehran. The IRGC and the Artesh fight each other. Opposition militias rise in Kurdish regions, Sistan-Baluchestan, and Arab Khuzestan. Iran becomes a collection of armed franchises with no central authority. This is the worst outcome for the United States, for the Iranian people, and for every neighboring state.

Either path ends the Islamic Republic. The only question is which arrives first.

Bottom Line
The regime cannot suppress protests it cannot pay its security forces to suppress. The IRGC cannot fight a war the state cannot fund. The clerical establishment cannot govern an apparatus that no longer answers to it.

Decapitation began on February 28 with the killing of Khamenei. It is now financial.

Two months ago the question was whether the regime could be defeated militarily. Today the question is whether it can pay itself through the next sixty days. Military pressure made the financial collapse possible. The financial collapse is what ends the regime.

The hardliners are hiding missiles for a final strike that will not save them. The IRGC is recruiting children. The clerical leadership has gone silent.

The regime draws its resilience not only from missiles but from a political-theological doctrine that fused Shi’ite theology with anti-imperialist history. At its core is the martyrdom of Imam Hussein at Karbala — the story of a small band fighting a mighty empire and choosing death over submission. That narrative has been turned into state ideology: injuries from an unjust tyrant do not break the faithful; they inspire them to keep fighting.

This is why the regime will not surrender. For its remaining hardliners, surrender is not defeat — it is betrayal of the founding myth. Death in battle against America and Israel is not loss. It is the highest reward.

The analysis of Iran's oil crisis you've requested is presented in the report below. The overall assessment indicates that, while the threat is severe, a full shutdown is likely to be deferred through technical workarounds, with the outcome hinging on whether Iran's political leadership can survive the acute social and economic pressures first.

---

## 🧠 Executive Summary: Iran's Oil Shutdown – A Timeline Analysis

Iran's economy, heavily reliant on oil revenues, is facing a sudden and severe external shock from a tightened US maritime blockade. The country is losing a vital source of income, with limited capacity to store the oil it continues to produce. This analysis finds that while the core claim of a potential shutdown is highly credible, the timeline of "13-16 days" is an optimistic scenario. In practice, Iran will likely use several workarounds—including floating storage and domestic refining—to delay a full-scale production cut by weeks or months. The primary short-term impact will be not on oil fields but on Iran's financial stability, driving inflation, unemployment, and social unrest, potentially forcing political change before a single well is shut.

---

## 📉 Section 1: Dissecting the Core Claim – Oil Revenue & Economic Lifeblood

The claim that oil accounts for **70-80 percent** of Iran's revenue is a reasonable estimate from recent years. In 2026, the share in the government's formal budget is lower (approx. **40%** ) due to the plummeting value of the rial. However, this **understates** total dependency, as the government also relies on funds from the National Development Fund (NDF), which gets 20% of oil revenues, and because Iran's semi-state actors like the IRGC derive substantial income directly from oil smuggling outside the budget. The $80.9 billion in 2022 goods exports further underscores this dominance. This creates a critical fiscal gap, forcing reliance on reserves and currency devaluation.

The revenue loss is staggering: the US blockade is estimated to cut off about **$150 million a day** in oil income. Iran earned approximately **$9 billion** from crude exports in the 40 days before the blockade. This windfall is now gone.

---

## ⛓️ Section 2: The Storage Crisis – Why the Clock is Ticking

The "13-16 day" timeline is based on a "perfect storm" scenario, but the situation is more fluid.

*   **"13-16 Days": The Mechanics of a Run on Storage**
    The estimate originates from the available **onshore storage capacity** for surplus oil. Iran has roughly 50–55 million barrels of onshore storage capacity, about **60%** of which is already filled, leaving ~20 million barrels of spare capacity. With surplus export volumes of **~1.5 million barrels per day** (bpd), this spare capacity would be exhausted in about **13 days** (20 million / 1.5 million = ~13 days). Once storage is full, wells must be shut in, risking permanent damage from water intrusion. One estimate gave a slightly more optimistic 16 days.

*   **Complicating Factors – The "Wriggle Room"**
    *   **Floating Storage:** Iran has a massive "floating storage" of oil on tankers at sea, estimated at **180-190 million barrels**, representing over $15 billion in deferred revenue. This acts as a significant buffer.
    *   **Variable Capacity & Production:** Estimates of total land storage capacity vary widely (e.g., 73 million vs. 122 million). Production is also variable, at around **3.06 million bpd** (down from 3.26 million). Domestic refineries consume roughly 2 million bpd of crude, leaving about 1 million bpd for export, not 1.5 million.

Thus, the **true "days to fill storage"** is not a fixed number but a range dependent on production cuts and the use of floating storage.

---

## 💥 Section 3: Beyond the Shutdown – The Immediate Economic War

Even without an immediate production shutdown, the economic and social impact is devastating.

*   **Economic Devastation**: The blockade is expected to wipe out an estimated **$435 million in daily economic activity**. Inflation was already at **47.5%** before the war. The rial has weakened sharply, with food prices rising up to sevenfold in recent months.
*   **Unemployment Crisis**: Massive job losses are already underway. An estimated **two million people could lose their jobs** as factories, services, and small businesses struggle. Major industries like steel and petrochemicals have halted. This is creating a humanitarian crisis and fueling civil unrest.
*   **Political Instability**: This is the most critical risk. The Iranian regime's legitimacy depends on its ability to provide basic economic security. The combination of hyperinflation, unemployment, and shortages of essential goods has historically triggered massive protests (e.g., 2019, 2022). The current crisis could prove existential for the regime.

---

## ⚔️ Section 4: The Strategic Chessboard – The Kharg Island Chokepoint

The blockade's effectiveness is amplified by the extreme concentration of Iran's oil infrastructure.

earnings and 23.7% of the national GDP, the closure of the Strait “zeroes this out overnight.”

IRAN: FROM ANCIENT EMPIRE TO THE FIRES OF 2026
A Detailed History of a Nation, Its Conflicts, and the War That Shook the World

THE ROOTS OF A GREAT CIVILISATION

Long before the word "Middle East" ever existed on any map, Iran stood as one of the oldest and most sophisticated civilisations humanity had ever produced. The Persians were not simply desert people. They were architects, poets, administrators, and warriors who built an empire so vast it stretched from modern day Greece all the way to the borders of India. Under Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BC, Persia became the first empire in recorded history to issue a declaration protecting the rights of conquered peoples. That document, carved on a clay cylinder, is considered by some scholars to be the world's first human rights charter. This is important context. It tells you that the people of Iran have always carried within them a profound sense of identity, dignity, and civilisational pride. That pride would later become both their greatest strength and a source of the tensions that led to the current war.

The Persian Empire fell to Alexander the Great, was later absorbed into various dynasties, and then came the arrival of Islam in the 7th century AD, which changed Iran fundamentally. The Arabs brought their religion, but the Iranians kept their language, their culture, and eventually developed a distinctly Persian form of Islam rooted in Shia theology. That Shia identity would become the cornerstone of the Islamic Republic that rose to power in 1979 and the source of its deepest rivalries in the region.

THE QAJAR AND PAHLAVI ERA: OIL, EMPIRE AND HUMILIATION

By the 19th and early 20th centuries, Iran was a weakened monarchy caught between two great powers, Britain and Russia, both of whom were hungry for influence and resources. The British discovered oil in Iran in 1908, and the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, which later became BP, began extracting Iran's enormous oil wealth while ordinary Iranians saw little to no benefit from it. This economic exploitation planted deep seeds of resentment against Western powers, seeds that have never fully been uprooted.

In 1951, Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, a democratically elected nationalist, moved to nationalise the oil industry and return Iran's oil revenues to its own people. The British government was outraged. Together with the United States CIA, they engineered a coup in 1953, known as Operation Ajax, which overthrew Mosaddegh and reinstated the Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, as the supreme authority. This moment is impossible to overstate in understanding Iran's view of America. To ordinary Iranians and to the revolutionaries who came after, 1953 was proof that the United States would always prioritise its own interests over Iranian democracy and sovereignty. It was a wound that never healed.

The Shah modernised Iran in many respects, pushing education, infrastructure, and women's rights, but he also ran a brutal secret police known as SAVAK, which tortured and imprisoned political opponents. He tried to reshape Iran in a Western image while suppressing Islamic and leftist movements. The contradiction was unsustainable.

1979: THE REVOLUTION THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING

On the morning of February 1, 1979, a bearded 76 year old cleric named Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini stepped off a plane in Tehran after 14 years of exile. The crowd that greeted him numbered in the millions. The Shah had fled weeks earlier. What followed was not just a change of government. It was a total revolution of identity. The Islamic Republic of Iran was declared. Sharia law became the foundation of governance. Women were required to wear the hijab. Political opponents were executed in the thousands. And the United States was declared the "Great Satan," enemy number one.

The seizure of the American Embassy in Tehran in November 1979, where 52 American diplomats were held hostage for 444 days, destroyed any remaining diplomatic goodwill between Washington and Tehran. America never forgot it. Iran never apologised for it.

THE IRAN-IRAQ WAR: BLOOD, SACRIFICE AND DEFIANCE

Barely a year into the revolution, Iraq's Saddam Hussein, backed financially and militarily by the United States, launched a full scale invasion of Iran in September 1980. He expected Iran to collapse quickly. It did not. What followed was eight years of devastating war that killed an estimated 500,000 Iranians and wounded over a million more. Iran used child soldiers, human wave attacks, and immense sacrifice to hold its ground. The war ended in 1988 in an exhausted stalemate, but it deeply shaped the Iranian national psyche. The generation that fought that war became the backbone of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the elite military force that would later carry out much of Iran's regional and nuclear ambitions.

Critically, the United States had provided chemical weapons intelligence to Saddam Hussein, and when he used chemical weapons against Iranian troops and Kurdish civilians, Washington said very little. For Iranians, this was another chapter in the story of American betrayal.

THE NUCLEAR PROGRAMME: A NATION'S RIGHT OR A GLOBAL THREAT?

Iran has maintained for decades that its nuclear programme is entirely peaceful, aimed at generating electricity and producing medical isotopes. The United States, Israel, and much of the Western world have never believed it. The evidence of uranium enrichment to levels well beyond what civilian energy requires, combined with Iran's secrecy about its facilities, convinced the world that Tehran was edging toward a nuclear weapon.

The IAEA discovered undeclared nuclear facilities in Iran in 2002, triggering years of international crisis. The UN imposed sanctions. Iran defied them. Diplomatic talks came and went. In 2015, under President Barack Obama, a landmark agreement called the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action was signed between Iran and six world powers. Iran agreed to limit its enrichment and submit to international inspections. In return, crippling economic sanctions were lifted. For a brief moment, it seemed as though the standoff might end.

Then Donald Trump became president of the United States in 2017.

TRUMP, MAXIMUM PRESSURE AND THE ROAD TO CONFLICT

In 2018, Trump unilaterally withdrew the United States from the JCPOA, calling it the "worst deal ever negotiated." He reimposed sweeping sanctions that strangled Iran's economy. Oil revenues collapsed. Inflation soared. Ordinary Iranians, not the regime, bore the heaviest burden of these sanctions. The Iranian currency, the rial, became almost worthless. Iran responded by slowly and deliberately increasing its uranium enrichment beyond the JCPOA limits, essentially daring the world to stop it.

In January 2020, Trump ordered the assassination of Iran's most powerful military commander, General Qasem Soleimani, in a drone strike near Baghdad airport. Soleimani was the architect of Iran's entire network of regional proxies, from Hezbollah in Lebanon to the Houthis in Yemen to militias in Iraq and Syria. His death sent shockwaves through the region and sent tens of millions of Iranians into the streets in grief and fury. Iran fired missiles at American bases in Iraq in retaliation. Nobody was killed, and both sides quietly stepped back from the edge. But the hatred deepened.

THE TWELVE DAY WAR OF 2025: THE FIRST EXPLOSION

When Trump returned to the White House for his second term in January 2025, the pressure on Iran intensified again. Negotiations stumbled. Israel, under Benjamin Netanyahu, grew increasingly impatient with the diplomatic route. Iran was now estimated to have enough 60 percent enriched uranium to produce multiple nuclear weapons if it chose to go further.

In June 2025, the United States and Israel launched what became known as Operation Midnight Hammer, a series of targeted strikes on Iran's key nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan. The strikes decimated those facilities. Iran retaliated. The fighting lasted twelve days before a ceasefire mediated by the United States and Qatar brought the guns briefly silent. But the ceasefire was always fragile. Iran's new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, continued to insist on Iran's right to enrich uranium. The underlying dispute had not been resolved. It had merely been paused.

FEBRUARY 28, 2026: OPERATION EPIC FURY AND THE START OF FULL WAR

The months between June 2025 and February 2026 were full of dangerous energy. Iran was rebuilding. Negotiations were ongoing but failing. American military forces were quietly massing in the region. On February 25, 2026, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi declared that a "historic" agreement to avoid conflict was "within reach." On February 27, Oman's foreign minister said a breakthrough had been reached and that peace was close. Talks were expected to resume on March 2.

They never happened.

On the morning of February 28, 2026, the world woke up to the news that the United States and Israel had launched a massive coordinated military assault on Iran under Operation Epic Fury. Nearly 900 joint strikes were carried out in just the first 12 hours. The attacks targeted Iranian missiles and air defenses, military infrastructure, and Iranian leadership. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the very first wave of strikes, along with dozens of other top Iranian officials.

The objectives stated by President Trump were four: preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, destroying its missile arsenal and production sites, degrading its proxy networks, and annihilating its navy, alongside a desired political outcome of regime change from within. According to the Washington Post and the New York Times, Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia Mohammed bin Salman had multiple phone calls with Trump urging him to attack Iran, and Trump's decision came after the Saudi Arabian and Israeli governments lobbied him repeatedly.

Iran did not collapse. It struck back ferociously, firing hundreds of missiles and thousands of drones across the entire region, targeting Gulf Arab states, American bases, and Israeli cities. Iran also moved to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow chokepoint through which a fifth of the world's oil supply travels, sending global fuel prices surging past $100 a barrel and triggering economic panic worldwide.

THE HUMAN COST AND GLOBAL SHOCKWAVES

The scale of devastation was breathtaking. Over 1,500 people were killed in Lebanon and 23 in Israel. The U.S. based rights group HRANA put the total killed in Iran at almost 3,400, including more than 1,600 civilians. Thirteen American service members were killed. One of the most shocking early moments was the destruction of a girls school near Bandar Abbas, killing around 170 children.

The Strait of Hormuz closure sent oil prices above $100 a barrel. Food supply chains to Gulf nations collapsed. Shipping companies rerouted around Africa, adding weeks and billions to global logistics costs. Countries across Asia that depend heavily on Gulf oil faced fuel rationing. The global economy, already under pressure from Trump's trade tariffs, took another brutal blow.

THE CEASEFIRE: FRAGILE, CONTESTED AND DEEPLY UNCERTAIN

After more than 40 days of relentless warfare, on April 8, 2026, the United States and Iran agreed to a two-week ceasefire mediated by Pakistan. Iran had rejected a 45-day framework and instead proposed its own 10-point peace plan. Trump announced the deal on Truth Social, calling Iran's plan "a workable basis on which to negotiate." Iran claimed victory, saying it had forced the United States to accept its demands.

But the ceasefire cracked almost immediately. Israel said it did not apply to its war against Hezbollah in Lebanon and launched what it called its largest wave of strikes on Lebanon since the war began, killing more than 250 people in a single day. Iran accused the United States of violating the ceasefire. Kuwait faced 28 Iranian drone attacks. The UAE faced 35 drone attacks. A fire broke out at Abu Dhabi's Habshan gas complex and a Saudi pipeline was directly hit by a drone.

Iran temporarily closed the Strait of Hormuz again in response to the Lebanon strikes, sending markets back into panic. Only a handful of ships managed to pass through the waterway in the first days of the so-called truce.

The Lebanese government declared a national day of mourning. The United Nations Secretary General condemned the civilian deaths. European leaders demanded that Lebanon be included in the ceasefire. Israel and the United States refused.

WHERE THINGS STAND TODAY: APRIL 10, 2026

As of today, American and Iranian delegations are expected to meet in Islamabad, Pakistan, under Pakistani mediation for the next phase of negotiations. Vice President JD Vance is leading the American delegation. Iran's delegation arrived in Pakistan on the evening of April 9.

The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to most shipping. Iran is charging tolls of over a million dollars per vessel for those it allows through. President Trump has warned Iran not to charge tankers. Iran's new supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei has declared Iran the winner of the war and is demanding compensation for the destruction caused by American and Israeli bombs.

Whether the Islamabad talks succeed or fail will determine whether the region slides back into full scale war or finds a path toward a lasting agreement. The world is watching. The people of Iran, who have suffered the most, are waiting. And the fires that have burned across the Middle East are only barely smouldering.

CONCLUSION: A CONFLICT DECADES IN THE MAKING

What is happening in 2026 is not something that started in February of this year. It started in 1953 when America overthrew a democratically elected Iranian leader. It deepened in 1979 when revolutionaries took American hostages. It was inflamed by the Iran-Iraq war, hardened by sanctions, and pushed over the edge by decades of mutual distrust between Tehran, Washington, and Tel Aviv. The nuclear issue was the trigger. But the gun had been loaded for 70 years.

No matter how this ends, the world will have changed because of it. The Strait of Hormuz will be seen differently. The power of nuclear ambiguity as a deterrent will be reexamined. And the question of whether military force can resolve what decades of diplomacy could not will hang over international relations for a very long time.

text:
Iran lost the conventional war on Day 1. Its Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his compound on February 28. Defense Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed. IRGC commander Mohammad Pakpour was killed. Defense Council Secretary Ali Shamkhani was killed. Four senior Ministry of Intelligence officials were killed. Iran's surface navy was largely eliminated within the opening days of strikes. Its air force was grounded. Its missile production facilities were struck. Its nuclear sites were targeted. The Israeli and American air campaigns achieved, at the military-tactical level, most of what they set out to achieve.

And then Iran did something its adversaries had not modelled with sufficient seriousness. It closed 21 miles of water.

On March 2, the IRGC officially closed the Strait of Hormuz. Not with a navy — its navy was gone. With mines laid from fishing boats. With GPS spoofing that affected over 1,650 vessels in a single day, causing their navigation systems to show them sailing over dry land. With fast-attack boats. With drone strikes on merchant ships. With the insurance market, which Iran understood would do the rest of the work without firing a single additional shot. War risk insurance premiums jumped tenfold within days. A single supertanker facing a 7.5–10% war risk premium on a hull worth hundreds of millions of dollars cannot economically transit the strait regardless of what any navy says. Traffic dropped 95% within days. Nearly 2,000 vessels stranded on both sides within a week.

By the time the dust of the conventional military defeat had settled, Iran was collecting tolls.

The IRGC toll system — which we have documented in full — requires ship operators to submit vessel ownership, cargo manifest, crew names, and AIS transponder history to an IRGC-linked intermediary. It charges approximately one dollar per barrel of oil cargo. A Very Large Crude Carrier carries up to 2 million barrels. A single crossing: up to $2 million. Payment in Chinese yuan through Kunlun Bank, outside SWIFT, or in cryptocurrency stable coins. Iran uses a five-tier ranking of "friendly nations" — China and Pakistan receive preferential rates. France's CMA CGM paid IRGC tolls in yuan on April 3. A Japanese shipping consortium paid on March 28. The IRGC was earning an estimated $139 million per day from this system by mid-March. Iranian legislators, meanwhile, were drafting permanent maritime legislation to codify the toll — transforming what began as a wartime measure into a permanent sovereign assertion over the world's most important waterway.

Iran's new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei — son of the killed Ali Khamenei — delivered his first public message confirming the strait will remain closed as a "tool of pressure." The legitimacy crisis the war was supposed to create has not materialized in the way its architects expected. Khamenei's death produced grief and solidarity within Iran's institutions, not collapse. The war that was supposed to trigger regime change has instead given the IRGC the clearest justification in its history for its own existence, its own power, and its own narrative.

What Iran's future holds is not comfortable. Its economy was already under severe strain — inflation exceeded 40% in 2025, and since the war began food inflation has surged to 105%. Bread and cereals are up 140% year on year. The central bank has issued a 10-million rial note — the largest denomination in its history. Iranian steel mills in Isfahan and Ahvaz were struck by Israeli airstrikes, with Khuzestan Steel reportedly requiring at least six months to repair. The economic pain inside Iran is real and severe.

But Iran has achieved something no one predicted it could achieve in 2026: it has demonstrated, to the entire world, that a country with no meaningful navy can close the circulatory system of the global economy, collect sovereign tolls from the shipping companies of its enemies, denominate those tolls in its ally's currency, and neutralize the most expensive military in human history — all while its Supreme Leader lay dead. The precedent that has been set is not about Iran alone. It is about what asymmetric geography and the willingness to absorb punishment can do to the assumptions on which the current world order rests.

In the years ahead, Iran will rebuild. It will rebuild under a new Supreme Leader who has inherited not a defeat but a documented victory over the insurance market, the global energy system, and American credibility simultaneously. Its Gulf neighbors — who lost far more economically — are furious at Tehran, and may move closer to Washington and Tel Aviv as a result. That realignment, if it materializes, is Iran's most significant long-term loss. But even that is not certain. Gulf states have nowhere else to go economically, because they are still trapped behind the same 21 miles.

Swim through the Noise - Why the market will price in a ceasefire between the US and Iran sooner than later

The market will price in certainty before you can stop being uncertain. 

The US is far less vulnerable to ongoing fighting than the headlines suggest, which makes the recent dip in US stocks look more like panic selling than anything rooted in lasting damage. 

On the other side, Iran, despite not wanting to back down, was already economically fragile and cannot sustain this conflict indefinitely. They may resist the idea of a ceasefire, but the mounting costs will eventually force them toward one to prevent total economic breakdown.

Part 1: The US Is Not Getting Hammered by the Oil Situation

We have built real energy strength over the past decade. US crude production stayed near record highs around 13.6 million barrels per day in 2025 and into 2026. Overall, we are a net exporter of petroleum products even if we still import some crude for refining. Imports from the Persian Gulf are minimal (less than 10% of total US crude imports), with the bulk coming from Canada (over 60%) and other nearby sources. That means direct reliance on the Strait of Hormuz is very low for American supply.

Higher oil prices triggered by the disruptions have actually been a net positive for many US companies. Domestic shale producers, refiners, and energy firms capture upside from the global spike. Gas prices at the pump rose, maybe 30-65 cents per gallon in different areas, and that adds some inflation pressure. Analysts adjusted recession odds slightly higher and talked about CPI possibly moving toward 4%, but those numbers assume a drawn-out shutdown. The US can release from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, increase domestic output where it makes sense, and let the market rebalance. Places like Europe and Asia, which depend much more heavily on Gulf oil and LNG, face far tougher stagflation risks. 

When the S&P 500 or Dow dips on war headlines, it feels like a short-term overreaction. The markets always overplay their hands early. Markets are baking in the nightmare scenario of a long Hormuz blockade, even as US production holds firm, SPR flows help, and energy / defense sectors stand to gain. This kind of volatility mirrors past Middle East flare-ups where the initial sell-off faded once the underlying US resilience became obvious. The real economic drag on America stays limited thanks to our domestic edge. That creates a potential buying opportunity in US equities when you focus on the fundamentals instead of fear.

Part 2: Iran Cannot Keep Fighting Indefinitely

Iran did not choose to start this war, but the conflict has accelerated problems that were already building. Last year, inflation ran above 40% (with food prices much higher in many cases), the rial kept sliding to new lows, and GDP contracted in the first half of the year despite modest oil sector growth. Sanctions had squeezed legitimate exports, pushing sales to China at steep discounts. Protests over living costs had flared up, and President Pezeshkian was pushing reforms while facing pushback from hardliners in the IRGC. The strikes on infrastructure, including energy sites like South Pars, made things worse fast. Iran's own oil and gas exports suffered from the same Hormuz disruptions they helped create. Global price jumps do not fully flow through to Tehran because of sanctions, forced discounts, and physical limits on shipments. Reports show staples doubling or tripling in price in short order, with broader shortages and activity dropping sharply. 

Pre-war outlooks from the World Bank and IMF already pointed to contraction and inflation potentially climbing toward 60% under tighter pressure. Add direct damage, mobilization, and lost revenue, and the hit deepens significantly. Pezeshkian has signaled the strain openly. Reports indicated warnings about the economy facing collapse within weeks without de-escalation. Hardliners push to keep using proxies and blockades for leverage, but the president and ordinary Iranians bear the daily pain of higher costs and instability. The regime relies on oil money for subsidies, military support, and keeping domestic stability. Prolonged fighting risks more unrest, faster currency collapse, and widening internal divisions. Their asymmetric capabilities get worn down without easy ways to rebuild them at scale. 

Iran may not want a ceasefire on terms that feel like defeat, and they continue to state tough conditions like reparations, recognition of rights, and guarantees against future strikes. But continuing the war gives them leverage through global disruption at a huge self-inflicted cost. Every extra week deepens poverty, tightens isolation, and raises the odds of popular backlash that threatens regime stability. A ceasefire would give breathing space to stabilize the currency, try resuming discounted exports, and ease some domestic anger. Past patterns show Iran has stepped back when economic pain crosses critical thresholds. They are signaling through intermediaries even amid public defiance because keeping the system intact matters more than endless attrition in the end.

The US can handle, and in some sectors even benefit from, higher energy prices thanks to our production strength, while equities mostly reflect temporary uncertainty rather than deep structural weakness. Iran, hit while already vulnerable, faces an economic squeeze that no Hormuz strategy can offset forever. Markets appear to be underestimating how much pressure Tehran is under and how that points toward eventual de-escalation. Once that reality sets in, the asymmetry should support a shorter conflict timeline and a more constructive outlook on US assets. 

The side with more endurance holds the edge here, and it is not Iran.

ΥΠΟΥΡΓΟΣ "ΑΜΥΝΑΣ" του Τρομοκράτους:
👉Now or Never: How to Finish the Job in Iran👈

The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has already achieved extraordinary  military results. The regime’s supreme leader is dead. Its nuclear  infrastructure is damaged. Its missile production has been severely  degraded. Its command structure is fractured. Across every major  military objective, decisive progress has been made.​
And yet, Iran has found a way to fight back. How? By closing the  Strait of Hormuz, and shifting the battlefield from military targets to  the global economy.

Roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and a  significant share of liquefied natural gas pass through that narrow  waterway. Iran brought traffic to a near standstill not with formal  naval blockade, but via selective drone strikes on tankers, the threat  of mines and anti-ship missiles, and the resulting collapse of insurance  coverage. Tanker movement has dropped by more than 90 percent. Brent  crude has surged to as much as $120 a barrel. One of the largest  disruptions to global energy supplies since the 1970s is now underway.

This  was a predictable move. Iran has threatened to close the Strait for  decades, and the logic was always clear: If the regime is struck hard  enough, it will use its geographic position to inflict economic pain on  the entire world. The question was never whether Iran would try. The  question is what we should do about it.

When military commanders  assess a situation, they examine three things: the environment, the  enemy’s capabilities, and their own.

First, the environment. The  Strait of Hormuz is narrow, crowded, and now likely partially mined,  especially in areas near the Gulf States. That means tankers are pushed  into a tighter navigational lane closer to the Iranian side, within  easier range of missiles, drones, and fast attack craft.

Second,  the enemy. Iran can employ a layered mix of threats along nearly 100  miles of coastline: naval mines, explosive boats, cruise and coastal  anti‑ship missiles, ballistic missiles, and unmanned aerial systems  launched from the shore and from depth inside its territory. Even if  many of these systems are degraded, enough will remain to keep any  transit under constant threat.

Third, our own  capabilities. The ships that transit the Strait are enormous commercial  vessels with civilian crews. The fundamental question is not only  whether the United States and its allies can reduce the threat they  face, but whether shipping companies will accept the risk, and whether  captains and crews will be willing to sail. One strike is enough to stop  traffic. The crews will refuse to board. The insurers will hesitate or  withdraw. The companies will refuse the liability. This risk alone has  been sufficient to halt the flow.

When you face this level  of operational complexity, you do not solve it by chasing every weapon  system. You change the enemy’s calculation. You must take from Iran  something it cannot afford to lose.

The first and most obvious target that meets that standard is Kharg Island.

Kharg  Island is a small strip of land in the northern Persian Gulf, roughly  comparable in size to lower Manhattan, sitting about 25 kilometers off  Iran’s coast and several hundred kilometers northwest of the Strait of  Hormuz. The main terminal for close to 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil  exports, Kharg Island is the economic backbone of the regime. It is  also, critically, the primary source of hard‑currency revenue for the  military and security services, which control and sell a significant  share of those exports.

Disrupting energy operations on Kharg  Island is regarded by analysts as a doomsday scenario for Iran’s  economy, with far‑reaching consequences. Iran’s economy depends in  practice on two main sectors: oil and gas. Disruption would trigger a  chain reaction throughout the energy system, creating acute shortages of  gasoline and diesel inside a country that sits on some of the largest  hydrocarbon reserves in the world. Iran would also lose billions of  dollars a month in oil income. Without the flow of dollars and yuan, the  central bank would struggle to defend the rial, driving hyperinflation  and eroding the savings of an entire society.

Economic pressure on  this scale would dramatically increase the likelihood of popular  unrest. Iran’s population has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to  take to the streets. The demonstrations of January 2026 were one of the  most significant since the 1979 revolution. A regime that cannot pay  its security forces or fuel its own economy faces a fundamentally  different internal reality.​ Its ability to support proxies and sleeper  cells throughout the Middle East, Europe, and the U.S. would also be  compromised.

The U.S. has already struck dozens of military  targets on Kharg Island while deliberately sparing the oil  infrastructure. President Trump has warned that those oil installations  will be next if Iran continues to interfere with shipping. But warnings  alone will not reopen the Strait. Iran’s leaders have already decided  that the global economic pain they are inflicting by closing Hormuz  outweighs the risk that Kharg’s facilities might be damaged.

The operational logic therefore points toward seizure, not destruction.

If  you bomb Kharg’s oil infrastructure, you destroy an asset that would  take years to rebuild and eliminate a potential source of leverage. But  if you seize the island, you control it. Iran cannot export a single  barrel without your permission. You’re able to tell Tehran: Open the  Strait and we discuss terms. Keep it closed and your oil revenue drops  to zero.

When a regime loses both its external leverage over the  global economy and its internal ability to buy time with money and fuel,  its options narrow. The same choke point Iran is using to pressure the  world can become the instrument that pressures the regime.

How,  though, would this operation work in practice? An amphibious assault on a  defended shore is one of the most demanding operations in modern  warfare. Militaries study landings like Normandy for a reason: They  require precise coordination across sea, air, and land domains, and they  leave the first waves of troops exposed if combat power does not  quickly build ashore. Success depends on integrating helicopters and  fixed‑wing aircraft, landing craft, ground forces, intelligence, and  constant protection against missile and drone attacks.

Kharg  Island, however, presents unique conditions. It is a small, isolated  objective, far from Iran’s main population centers, ringed by waters the  United States already dominates from the air and sea. American forces  can approach from multiple directions and bring significant combat power  to bear in the opening hours. The primary danger does not come from the  relatively limited Iranian forces on the island itself, but from  long‑range missiles, drones, and other strike systems positioned deeper  inside Iran.

And yes, there are risks. Any operation to seize  Kharg would require thousands of troops, sustained air and naval  support, and detailed intelligence, and it would carry a real and  expected cost in human life. Iran would also target every reachable  energy facility across the Gulf, a campaign already underway.

But  the conditions in this case tilt the balance in favor of action. The  U.S. has overwhelming air superiority. Maritime advantage around the  island is significant but partial. Small assault craft can be airlifted  to neighboring countries and reach Kharg directly. Bringing larger  warships into position, however, would require transiting the Strait of  Hormuz itself, which is possible but carries risks. In military terms,  this is a difficult operation, but it is not an impossible one.

President  Trump has set up the U.S. for this option. By signaling willingness to  explore a diplomatic agreement with Iran, he has shown both the American  people and the international community that he is prepared to  compromise if Iran meets core demands. At the same time, he has set  clear conditions: the transfer of enriched uranium, the reopening of the  Strait of Hormuz, and effective guarantees against renewed nuclear and  regional aggression.​

In giving Iran days, not months, to meet  these conditions, he buys time for U.S. forces and their allies to  prepare and finalize operational plans. That time is not a concession.  It is an investment in readiness, and it strengthens the president’s  position domestically and internationally for whatever comes next. If  Iran accepts the terms, the objectives are achieved without seizing  Kharg. If Iran refuses, the president will have both the legitimacy and  the capability to act.

The question, then, is not whether a  diplomatic formula can be imagined. It is whether this regime will agree  to conditions it will portray at home as surrender. Everything we know  about Tehran’s behavior suggests that is unlikely.​

As  long as Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz, the regime retains a veto  over the global economy. As long as the world’s energy supply remains  hostage to Iranian weapons deployed along a hundred miles of coastline,  the destruction of nuclear and missile sites will be overshadowed by an  economic crisis that erodes the will to finish the job.

Kharg  Island is the key that resolves this equation. It accelerates the  economic and political pressure that may finally produce the internal  change the Iranian people have sought for decades. And it sends a  message air strikes alone cannot deliver: The U.S. is committed to a  decisive outcome, and it is not going home without one.

On the  strategic chessboard of this war, Kharg Island is the next piece. It may  be the move that decides the conflict. If it is going to be made, it  must be made now.
